newsitem.title: USA: U.S. doesn't recognize new premier in Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. doesn't recognize new premier in Cambodia.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday it was "very concerned" by a decision to make Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot the country's co-prime minister and did not recognise him in that position.

A dissident faction of ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party said on Wednesday it would nominate Ung Huot as the prince's replacement. Ung Huot said he was willing to take the job.

Second Prime Minister Hun Sen overthrew Ranariddh on July 6 but said he wanted the coalition between his Cambodian People's Party and FUNCINPEC to remain in place and the royalist party to choose a new first prime minister.
"We are very concerned about the decision this morning to make the Cambodian foreign minister co-prime minister with Hun Sen," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"We see no evidence whatsoever that FUNCINPEC has met...and has elected on a free basis, on a democratic basis, a successor to Prince Ranariddh," he told a news briefing.

"We urge the authorities in Phnom Penh to refrain from announcing a new first prime minister until Prince Ranariddh's political party has an opportunity to make a reasoned decision on this matter, free of coercion, free of intimidation."
Ranariddh left Cambodia on the eve of Hun Sen's takeover and has not returned.

The U.S. Senate also voted 99-0 late on Wednesday to halt U.S. aid to Cambodia until the secretary of state certified that the Cambodian government was established by free and fair elections, and not by force or coup d'etat.

The measure also called upon the secretary to certify that Cambodia has discontinued all political violence, established an independent election commission, guaranteed free speech and assembly, and stopped collaborating with narcotics smugglers.
The measure was approved as an amendment to the pending $13.2 billion fiscal 1998 foreign aid appropriations bill.
Washington allocated $35 million in aid to the Southeast Asian state for fiscal 1997, which ends in September.

Burns said the United States had dealt "very cooperatively" with Ung Huot as foreign minister in the past, "but we don't recognise him as first prime minister, we recognise Prince Ranariddh as first prime minister."
It was not for Ung Huot to accept the job without Ranariddh expressing an opinion, he said.
Burns said the United States was also "very deeply troubled" by reports of killings of Ranariddh supporters in Cambodia.
As many as 40 Cambodians have been killed since Ranariddh's overthrow but it was not clear if the killings were part of a planned purge, a diplomatic source said Wednesday in Phnom Penh.

"We're deeply concerned about the reports of the executions and other reports about intimidation of Cambodians who have been working to build a civil society, people like journalists and labour union organisers, Cambodian citizens who work for private voluntary organisations," Burns said.

"Any attempt to arrest or to intimidate or to execute people because of their political views has to be rejected by the United States. It is contrary to all decent standards of international behaviour, and it's contrary to the Cambodian constitution."
Burns said the U.S. ambassador to Cambodia, Kenneth Quinn, had conveyed Washington's concerns directly to Hun Sen and would continue to do so.
